title: 2 Chronicles 13:13–22
context: Jeroboam sets an ambush, and Judah finds itself attacked from front and rear. Judah cries to the LORD, the priests blow the trumpets, and at Judah’s shout God strikes Jeroboam and Israel. The Chronicler says Judah prevailed because they relied on the LORD. Abijah takes Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron with their villages, and Jeroboam never regains strength; the LORD strikes him and he dies. Abijah grows strong and has a large family, and his acts are recorded in the commentary of the prophet Iddo. The large army figures in this chapter are given as the text states them and are read in more than one way.

verses.text: But Jeroboam caused an ambush to come about behind them; so they were before Judah, and the ambush was behind them.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeroboam sets an ambush behind Judah. Arminian readers note that Jeroboam responds to the speech with military strategy rather than repentance, choosing to press the attack.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the trap as making Judah’s deliverance all the clearer as God’s work. Shared ground: the verse sets up a desperate situation that leads Judah to cry out to the LORD.

verses.text: When Judah looked back, behold, the battle was before and behind them; and they cried to the LORD, and the priests sounded with the trumpets.
verses.arminianNotes: Judah, surrounded, cries to the LORD, and the priests sound the trumpets. Arminian readers see a real turning to God in distress, a pattern the Chronicler commends throughout.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the trumpets fulfilling the word of 13:12 and Numbers 10:9. Both traditions read the cry as dependence on God at the moment of greatest danger, a point fully shared.

verses.text: Then the men of Judah gave a shout. As the men of Judah shouted, God struck Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah and Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: Judah shouts, and God strikes Jeroboam and Israel. Arminian readers note that the victory is credited directly to God in response to his people’s cry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God acting decisively for the house of David as Abijah had said. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as God giving victory, with Judah’s shout as an act of faith rather than the cause of the outcome.

verses.text: The children of Israel fled before Judah, and God delivered them into their hand.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel flees, and God delivers them into Judah’s hand. Arminian readers note the brief, direct statement that the outcome came from God rather than from Judah’s numbers or skill.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the deliverance as consistent with God’s faithfulness to his covenant with David. Both traditions read the verse simply as God granting victory to the people who called on him.

verses.text: Abijah and his people killed them with a great slaughter, so five hundred thousand chosen men of Israel fell down slain.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel’s losses are put at five hundred thousand chosen men. Arminian readers stress the scale of the defeat the Chronicler wants to convey, while recognizing that interpreters handle such totals differently.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same and focus on the narrative point: Israel suffers a crushing defeat. Shared ground: both traditions state the number as the text gives it and avoid speculative harmonization.

verses.text: Thus the children of Israel were brought under at that time, and the children of Judah prevailed, because they relied on the LORD, the God of their fathers.
verses.arminianNotes: Judah prevailed because they relied on the LORD, the God of their fathers. Arminian readers see God honoring his people’s trust, a principle the Chronicler stresses across these chapters.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see reliance on God as itself the fruit of his grace in his people. Shared ground: both traditions agree that God honors trust and judges self-reliance; neither treats this verse as a soteriological fork.

verses.text: Abijah pursued Jeroboam, and took cities from him: Bethel with its villages, Jeshanah with its villages, and Ephron with its villages.
verses.arminianNotes: Abijah pursues Jeroboam and takes Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron with their villages. Arminian readers note the irony of Bethel, the site of one of Jeroboam’s calves, passing to Judah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the captured cities as a sign of God’s judgment on Jeroboam’s false worship. Both traditions note that the locations of Jeshanah and Ephron are uncertain, and that Bethel later appears again under Israel.

verses.text: Jeroboam didn’t recover strength again in the days of Abijah. The LORD struck him, and he died.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeroboam does not recover strength in Abijah’s days, and the LORD strikes him, and he dies. Arminian readers note that the text does not say exactly when he died; 1 Kings 15:9 dates Asa’s accession to Jeroboam’s twentieth year.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s hand in Jeroboam’s end. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the Chronicler’s verdict on Jeroboam, while leaving the precise timing to the parallel accounts without harmonizing them.

verses.text: But Abijah grew mighty and took for himself fourteen wives, and became the father of twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters.
verses.arminianNotes: Abijah grows mighty, takes fourteen wives, and has twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters. Arminian readers note that the Chronicler records his strength and large family as signs of his prosperity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the multiplying of wives sits uneasily with Deuteronomy 17:17, though the text does not comment. Both traditions read the verse as reported without explicit evaluation.

verses.text: The rest of the acts of Abijah, his ways, and his sayings are written in the commentary of the prophet Iddo.
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of Abijah’s acts, ways, and sayings are written in the commentary of the prophet Iddo. Arminian readers note that the Chronicler draws on sources no longer available, naming a prophet’s record here.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the reference to prophetic writings as part of the Chronicler’s concern with God’s word through prophets. Shared ground: the source is not extant, and both traditions read the verse as a standard closing note.
